newsitem.title: USA: Christopher's China visit aims to help mend ties.
newsitem.headline: Christopher's China visit aims to help mend ties.

text.p: In one of his last major acts as secretary of state, Warren Christopher this weekend flies to Beijing to try to ensure that Sino-American ties, which frayed badly during his tenure, are on the mend.

U.S. officials consider managing ties with China to be one of the major foreign policy challenges facing the United States into the 21st century. Many irritants remain and they will be addressed in day-long meetings on Nov. 20 involving Christopher, Chinese President Jiang Zemin, Foreign Minister Qian Qichen and other senior officials.

A dramatic example was the case of prominent dissident Wang Dan, whose 11-year prison sentence for subversion was upheld on Friday -- days before Christopher's arrival -- by a Chinese court after deliberations lasting just 10 minutes.
The State Department expressed disappointment at the verdict, called for Wang's release and stressed that human rights in general would be raised by Christopher in his talks.

Other concerns involve trade, Taiwan and China's sales of nuclear technology and arms to countries like Iran and Pakistan. But the emphasis was expected to be on the positive as both sides continued the long climb back from the abyss where they teetered for much of President Bill Clinton's first four years in office.

With Clinton elected to a second term, his administration was intensifying efforts to revive a dialogue and ensure the two major powers can manage their often-serious differences while cooperating on areas of convergence like North Korea.

U.S. officials say they believe the Chinese have similar goals. Christopher's only trip to Beijing as secretary of state more than two years ago was a disaster, in large measure because of disputes over human rights issues.

Since then, Clinton has unlinked human rights from Most Favourable Nation trade status for China and pursued progress on various fronts with Beijing, irrespective of what was happening on other tracks.

The relationship -- shaky after Beijing's 1989 crackdown on pro-democracy protesters in Tiananmen Square -- worsened in 1995 when Clinton let Taiwan President Lee Teng-hui pay a private visit to the United States. Officials have worked since then to restore confidence and regular dialogues.
After Beijing, Christopher will stop in Shanghai, then fly to Manila for an Asian-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum summit. Clinton and Jiang will meet on Nov. 24 on the fringes of the summit.

The two countries have been discussing an exchange of summit visits by their leaders and could announce a timetable in Manila. Officials have said they expect Vice President Gore to visit China. A Jiang visit to Washington might come next, with Clinton visiting Beijing later.

Expectations for Christopher's Beijing visit were modest, mainly to ensure a dialogue that has been gaining strength in recent months continues. Although he has announced his resignation, U.S. officials say his lame duck status will not dilute his effectiveness since he represents a leader with a new mandate.

Officials say there could be incremental progress on a 1985 agreement granting China access to U.S. nuclear technology that has not taken effect because of concerns over Beijing's assistance to countries without safeguards for nuclear facilities.

Assistant Secretary of State Winston Lord said China had not yet made enough progress in curbing troublesome nuclear sales to warrant access to billions of dollars worth of American-made nuclear reactors under the agreement.

But other officials said both sides were determined to move forward in this area and could agree on a schedule for taking action. Washington was still working to obtain the kind of assurances and commitments it needs to be convinced China is set on this course, they said.
Lord said the United States was looking for signs that China was now serious about engaging in negotiations on gaining membership in the World Trade Organisation.
